MANILA, Philippines — The country’s first mid-merit natural gas auction could fetch offers exceeding P7 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), with fuel costs still to be recovered separately from consumers.
Under its proposed resolution, the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) has set different gas auction thresholds (GATs) depending on the technology and whether the power plants are existing facilities or new builds.
The ERC proposed a GAT or maximum allowable price offer of P7.16 per kWh for new-build combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs), which use both gas and steam to generate electricity.
For new-build open-cycle gas turbines, which rely solely on gas, the proposed ceiling is P4.45 per kWh.
Offers from new-build gas reciprocating engines, which generate electricity through large internal combustion engines, would be capped at P6.79 per kWh.
Existing CCGTs in Luzon, meanwhile, would have lower auction price thresholds. The proposed GAT is P2.76 per kWh for Lot 1, covering 1,400 megawatts, and P2.66 per kWh for Lot 2, covering 500 MW.
The GAT is calculated based on the assumed mid-merit operating level that will allow a power plant to recover its investment and earn the required return over its useful life.
In computing the preliminary GAT prices, the ERC used a net capacity factor of 42 percent, in line with the Department of Energy (DOE)’s terms of reference.
The GAT price covers only the cost of the plant itself: building and financing it, operating and maintaining it, overhead, taxes and a reasonable return to investors.
Fuel costs, which include the price of gas and capped landed logistics costs, are excluded from the proposed price ceilings. These are recovered monthly based on actual costs, subject to an ERC-set benchmark.
Recently, the regulator approved the gas auction implementing rules, which set the price ceiling, fuel cost safeguards and the payment system for the bidding round.
“The DOE runs the auction. The ERC makes sure the price ceiling is fair, that fuel costs are checked against market benchmarks, and that plants are paid only for power they actually deliver,” ERC chairman and CEO Francis Saturnino Juan said.
For this landmark auction, the DOE seeks to attract 3,800 MW of mid-merit gas capacity.
Mid-merit plants play a vital role in keeping the power grid stable by bridging the gap between always-on baseload generation and peak-demand sources. Such facilities can quickly adjust their output in response to fluctuations in demand.

deepDives.summary: The peso may find temporary relief from easing oil prices and stronger holiday remittances, but a sustained recovery remains unlikely unless crude prices fall below $70 per barrel and the country’s external deficits narrow, according to Bank of America and Citi.

MANILA, Philippines — The peso may find temporary relief from easing oil prices and stronger holiday remittances, but a sustained recovery remains unlikely unless crude prices fall below $70 per barrel and the country’s external deficits narrow, according to Bank of America (BofA) and Citi.
In a report, BofA emerging Asia forex strategist Abhay Gupta said the local currency could stabilize near current levels as declining oil prices ease pressure on the Philippines’ import bill.
However, Gupta warned that the peso’s medium-term outlook would remain weak unless Brent crude falls to around $70 per barrel and the country’s basic balance deficit narrows to two to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
The basic balance measures the combined position of the current account and foreign direct investment flows, providing an indication of the country’s underlying external financing needs.
BofA noted that the Philippines’ current account deficit, which reflects the gap between money flowing into and out of the country through trade, income and transfers, widened to 6.3 percent of GDP in the first half from 3.5 percent in 2025.
Energy imports rose to 4.5 percent of GDP as of September from 3.4 percent last year, while weaker business process outsourcing revenues and slower remittances added pressure.
BofA expects seasonal remittance inflows ahead of Christmas to provide additional support, particularly in November and early December.
Similarly, Citi chief Asia economist Johanna Chua said the peso remained vulnerable to oil price movements and could underperform other Asian currencies.
“Peso is very sensitive to oil. So that is something that we obviously need to watch very closely,” Chua said during a media briefing.
Citi expects the peso to reach around 64 per dollar by March 2027, reflecting continued pressure from global dollar strength and the country’s external imbalances.
The peso hit a record low of 64.17 to $1 on Oct. 27 but rallied back to the 62 to $1 level.
Chua said Asian currencies benefiting from artificial intelligence-related investments and strong current account surpluses were better positioned than the peso.
Meanwhile, BofA said the Philippines’ inclusion in JPMorgan’s Government Bond Index-Emerging Markets could attract $4 billion to $5 billion in passive investment flows over 10 months beginning January 2027.
However, it cautioned that foreign exchange weakness, elevated interest rates and market liquidity constraints could delay or reduce these inflows.
BofA also said the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas retained room to smooth excessive currency volatility despite the decline in its foreign exchange reserves.

MANILA, Philippines — Economists expect the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to raise interest rates further despite the economy’s sharp slowdown, as stubborn inflation continues to squeeze household spending and threatens to delay a recovery.
The country’s gross domestic product (GDP) grew by just 2.1 percent in the third quarter, down from 2.4 percent in the preceding quarter and four percent a year earlier, the Philippine Statistics Authority reported on Monday.
GDP, the total value of goods and services produced in the country, expanded at its slowest pace since the pandemic and missed the market’s 3.1-percent forecast.
Economists from HSBC, Bank of America (BofA) and Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) said weak demand and rising living costs have complicated the BSP’s task of controlling inflation without further undermining growth.
HSBC economist Aris Dacanay said the disappointing GDP figure reduced the likelihood of another aggressive 50-basis-point rate hike in December, but did not eliminate the need for tightening.
Dacanay expects a smaller 25-basis-point increase to 5.75 percent next month, which he believes would end the central bank’s tightening cycle.
BofA expects another 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by a similar adjustment in February 2027, taking the benchmark rate to six percent.
BPI lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. likewise said additional increases remain likely, warning that pausing too early could allow inflation to become more entrenched and complicate the eventual recovery.
Household consumption grew only 2.4 percent in the third quarter, its weakest non-pandemic expansion since 2010, according to HSBC.
The Ayala-led bank noted that consumer spending rose 8.5 percent in nominal terms, indicating that much of the increase reflected higher prices rather than more goods and services purchased.
Dacanay also pointed to a confidence shock following investigations into flood-control projects that curtailed infrastructure disbursements. He said the shock had proved “large and long-lasting,” even as construction demand began improving.
Investment contracted by 0.2 percent, an improvement from the previous quarter’s 8.8-percent drop, while agriculture shrank 4.8 percent. Exports and government consumption grew 8.6 percent and 6.8 percent, respectively, but failed to offset weaker domestic demand.
The outlook remains subdued as BofA expects growth to improve slightly to 2.6 percent in the fourth quarter and 3.5 percent in 2027, from the projected 2.5 percent this year.
HSBC forecasts growth at 3.2 percent this year and 4.8 percent next year, although it warned the latest GDP result poses downside risks to both projections.
BofA sees inflation easing to 5.2 percent next year from six percent in 2026, but remaining above the BSP’s two to four percent target range until late 2027.
HSBC urged faster implementation of foreign-funded infrastructure projects and lower food import barriers to ease prices and revive consumer demand.

quickHits.title: 2026, 2027 economic targets face review, Palace says
quickHits.summary: THE government will review its economic growth, inflation and exchange rate targets for 2026 and 2027 next month…
reasons: reader relevance 2/3: Government to review 2026-2027 economic targets

article.text:
THE government will review its economic growth, inflation and exchange rate targets for 2026 and 2027 next month following weaker-than-expected third-quarter growth, Malacañang said on Tuesday.
“In line with the recommendations of the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev), the targets for 2026 and 2027, including GDP growth, inflation and the peso exchange rate, will be reviewed,” Palace Press Officer Clarissa A. Castro told reporters.
The Development Budget Coordination Committee (DBCC) will meet in early December to reassess the country’s macroeconomic assumptions and targets, she added.
“The government is pursuing projects and programs to ease inflationary pressures so they do not have a significant effect on the economy,” Ms. Castro said.
The Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is monitoring commodity prices, which are expected to remain stable through the end of the year, she said.
The government is also working to ensure adequate supplies of food and petroleum products to prevent shortages that could disrupt economic activity.
Third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) came in at 2.1%.
“We know what happened. The issue of the Middle East crisis is still there, and so is the big effect of a very strong El Niño,” Ms. Castro said, pointing to continuing pressures on the economy.

offbeat.title: 2020: Typhoon Vamco makes landfall in Luzon and several offshore islands, killing 67 people. The storm causes the worst floods in the region since Typhoon Ketsana in 2009.
offbeat.summary: Typhoon Vamco makes landfall in Luzon and several offshore islands, killing 67 people. The storm causes the worst floods in the region since Typhoon Ketsana in 2009.

article.text:
Typhoon Vamco,[nb 1] known in the Philippines as Typhoon Ulysses, was a powerful, deadly, and very destructive Category 4-equivalent typhoon that struck the Philippines and Vietnam in mid-November 2020. It also caused the worst flooding in Metro Manila since Typhoon Ketsana in 2009. The twenty-second named storm and tenth typhoon of the 2020 Pacific typhoon season, Vamco originated as a tropical depression northwest of Palau, where it slowly continued its northwest track until it made landfall in Quezon. After entering the South China Sea, Vamco further intensified in the South China Sea until it made its last landfall in Vietnam.
Vamco made its first landfall in the Philippines near midnight on November 11 in the Quezon province as a Category 2-equivalent typhoon. The typhoon brought heavy rains to Central Luzon and nearby provinces, including Metro Manila, the national capital. As the typhoon crossed the country, dams from all around Luzon neared their spilling points, forcing dam operators to release large amounts of water into their impounds. As the Magat Dam approached its spilling point, all seven of its gates were opened to prevent dam failure, which overflowed the Cagayan River and caused widespread floods in Cagayan and Isabela. After entering the South China Sea, Vamco further intensified until it reached its brief peak as a Category 4-equivalent typhoon. offbeat.title: 2002: A Fokker F27 Friendship operating as Laoag International Airlines Flight 585 crashes into Manila Bay shortly after takeoff from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, killing 19 people.
offbeat.summary: A Fokker F27 Friendship operating as Laoag International Airlines Flight 585 crashes into Manila Bay shortly after takeoff from Ninoy Aquino International Airport, killing 19 people.

article.text:
The Fokker F27 Friendship is a turboprop airliner developed and manufactured by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker. It is the most numerous post-war aircraft manufactured in the Netherlands; the F27 was also one of the most successful European airliners of its era. As a result it became the best-selling European turboprop airliner.[1]
The F27 was developed during the early 1950s with the intent of producing a capable successor to the earlier piston engine-powered airliners that had become commonplace on the market, such as the Douglas DC-3. A key innovation of the F27 was the adoption of the Rolls-Royce Dart turboprop engine, which produced substantially less vibration and noise, thus providing improved conditions for passengers. Another major comfort feature was cabin pressurisation. Innovative manufacturing techniques were also employed in the aircraft's construction.
On 24 November 1955, the F27 made its maiden flight; on 19 November 1958, the type was introduced to revenue service. Shortly after its introduction, the F27 was recognised as being a commercial success. Under a licensing arrangement reached between Fokker and the U.S. aircraft manufacturer Fairchild, the F27 was manufactured in the United States by the latter; Fairchild went on to independently develop a stretched version of the airliner, which was designated as the Fairchild FH-227.
